train.content: what is data lake vs data warehouse?

Data warehouse: structured, processed data optimized for analytics queries. Schema-on-write — define schema before loading data. Star/snowflake schema. SQL-based querying. Examples: Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks SQL. Use for: business intelligence, reporting, dashboards, SQL analytics. Data lake: raw, unprocessed data in any format (structured, semi-structured, unstructured). Schema-on-read — interpret data when querying. Store everything — logs, images, JSON, CSV, Parquet. Examples: S3, Azure Data Lake, Google Cloud Storage. Use for: machine learning (need raw data), data exploration, archive/compliance. Data lakehouse (modern approach): combines benefits of both. Structured tables on top of data lake storage. Delta Lake (Databricks), Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi. ACID transactions on data lake files. Query with SQL and ML tools. Modern data architecture: sources → ingestion (Fivetran, Airbyte) → data lake (S3, raw storage) → transformation (Spark, dbt) → data warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery) → BI (Looker, Metabase). Or with lakehouse: sources → ingestion → lakehouse (Delta Lake on S3) → both SQL analytics and ML. Key formats: Parquet (columnar, compressed — standard for analytics), ORC (Hadoop ecosystem), Avro (row-based, schema evolution), Delta (Parquet + transaction log). For most companies: start with a data warehouse (Snowflake/BigQuery). Add data lake when you have ML needs or need to store raw data economically.

train.content: what is edge cases in software development?

Edge cases are unusual or extreme inputs/conditions that software must handle. Categories: boundary values (0, -1, MAX_INT, empty string, null), empty states (empty list, no results, first-time user), concurrent access (two users editing same resource), network conditions (timeout, partial response, connection drop), large inputs (1 million items, very long strings), unicode and encoding (emojis, RTL text, multi-byte characters, zero-width characters), time zones and dates (DST transitions, leap years, year 2038 problem, different calendars), permissions (accessing another user's data, expired tokens), race conditions (double-click submit, back button after form submission). How to find edge cases: boundary value analysis (test at limits: 0, 1, max-1, max), equivalence partitioning (group inputs into classes, test each), think adversarially (how would a malicious user abuse this?), review production errors (real users find edge cases you missed), property-based testing (QuickCheck, Hypothesis — generate random inputs, verify properties hold). Best practices: validate at system boundaries (API inputs, form submissions), fail gracefully (show user-friendly errors, not stack traces), log edge cases (learn from unexpected inputs), write regression tests for edge cases found in production. Gorkem's projects benefit from edge case consideration — phishing detection needs to handle unusual domain formats, facelock handles varying lighting conditions.

train.content: what is open source business models?

Open source projects need sustainable funding. Models: Open Core: core is open source, premium features are proprietary. GitLab (CI/CD features in paid tiers), Elastic (security features), Grafana (enterprise plugins). Most common model. SaaS/Hosted: open source software, charge for hosted version. MongoDB Atlas, Redis Cloud, Supabase. Convenience and managed operations justify the cost. Support and Services: free software, charge for support, consulting, training. Red Hat (enterprise Linux support), Canonical (Ubuntu). Requires large install base. Dual Licensing: open source (AGPL) for community, commercial license for enterprises that don't want copyleft obligations. MySQL (Oracle), MongoDB (SSPL). Marketplace/Extensions: free platform, charge for plugins or marketplace listings. WordPress, Shopify. Sponsorship/Donations: GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective, Patreon. Works for small projects, rarely sustains large ones. Foundations: Linux Foundation, Apache Foundation, CNCF. Corporate sponsors fund development. Cloud provider threat: AWS/Google/Cloud take open source, offer managed versions, don't contribute back. Led to license changes: MongoDB (SSPL), Elastic (SSPL → back to open), Redis (source-available). SSPL and BSL (Business Source License) restrict cloud providers while keeping code viewable. Choose based on: target audience (developers vs enterprises), competitive landscape, growth stage. Most successful: open core + SaaS combination.
train.thinking: Open source, business model, open core, SaaS, dual licensing, sponsorship, SSPL, sustainability.

train.content: what is serverless architecture patterns?

Serverless patterns for building applications without managing servers. API pattern: API Gateway + Lambda functions. Each endpoint is a separate Lambda. Benefits: pay per request, auto-scaling, no server management. Frameworks: Serverless Framework, SST, AWS SAM. Fan-out pattern: one event triggers multiple parallel Lambda functions. S3 upload triggers: resize image + generate thumbnail + extract metadata simultaneously. Event processing: Lambda triggered by SQS/SNS/EventBridge. Process events asynchronously with built-in retry and dead letter queues. Scheduled tasks: CloudWatch Events/EventBridge triggers Lambda on cron schedule. Replace traditional cron jobs. Step Functions: orchestrate multiple Lambda functions into workflows. State machines with branching, parallel execution, error handling, retries. Good for complex business processes (order processing, data pipelines). Data processing: Lambda triggered by DynamoDB Streams or Kinesis. Real-time data transformation and enrichment. Challenges: cold starts (mitigate with provisioned concurrency or SnapStart), vendor lock-in (abstract with frameworks), 15-minute timeout (use Step Functions for long processes), local development (use SAM CLI, LocalStack), observability (use X-Ray, CloudWatch, Lumigo). Cost optimization: right-size memory (more memory = faster execution = less cost sometimes), use ARM64 (Graviton — 20% cheaper), minimize package size (faster cold starts). Serverless is not always cheaper — for consistent high traffic, containers (ECS/Fargate) may be more cost-effective.

train.content: what is API design principles?

Good API design makes APIs intuitive, consistent, and maintainable. Consistency: use the same patterns everywhere. If /users returns a list, /orders should too. Same pagination format, same error format, same naming convention. Naming: use nouns for resources (/users, /orders), plural for collections. Use kebab-case for URLs (/user-profiles), camelCase for JSON fields (firstName). Versioning: /api/v1/users — include version in URL for clarity. Error handling: consistent error format with code, message, and details. Use appropriate HTTP status codes. Include actionable error messages ('Email is required' not 'Validation failed'). Pagination: provide total count, next/previous links. Cursor-based for large datasets. Filtering: query parameters for filtering (?status=active&sort=-created_at). Rate limiting: include limit headers (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining). HATEOAS: include links to related resources and available actions in responses. Idempotency: support idempotency keys for POST requests. Documentation: OpenAPI/Swagger spec, interactive playground, code examples in multiple languages. Backward compatibility: never remove fields, add new fields as optional, version when breaking changes are needed. Design for the consumer — the best API is one that developers can use correctly without reading documentation. Gorkem's projects follow REST principles for clean API interfaces.
train.thinking: API design, consistency, naming, error handling, pagination, versioning, HATEOAS, REST.

train.content: what is micro-frontends?

Micro-frontends apply microservices principles to frontend development. Instead of one monolithic frontend, split into independently deployable frontend applications. Each team owns a slice of the UI end-to-end (frontend + backend). Approaches: Build-time composition: npm packages for shared components. Simple but coupled deployments. Run-time composition via iframes: strong isolation but limited communication and styling challenges. Run-time composition via JavaScript: Module Federation (Webpack 5) — load remote modules at runtime. Most popular approach. Each micro-frontend is a separate webpack build that exposes and consumes modules. Web Components: framework-agnostic custom elements. Each micro-frontend as a custom element. Server-side composition: Nginx/reverse proxy assembles page from multiple services. Edge-side includes (ESI). Benefits: independent deployments (team A deploys without team B), technology flexibility (React for one section, Vue for another), team autonomy, smaller codebases. Challenges: shared state management, consistent design system, performance (multiple framework instances), complexity, cross-cutting concerns (auth, routing). When to use: large organizations with multiple frontend teams, independently evolving products within one UI. When NOT to use: small teams, single product, when the overhead isn't justified. Most teams don't need micro-frontends — a well-structured monolithic frontend with clear module boundaries works better for smaller teams.

train.content: what is technical leadership?

Technical leadership is influence without authority — guiding technical direction, mentoring engineers, and ensuring quality without being everyone's boss. Responsibilities: technical vision (where should the architecture evolve?), decision making (choose technologies, patterns, trade-offs), mentoring (help engineers grow through code review, pairing, guidance), communication (translate business needs to technical plans and vice versa), quality (set standards, review designs, catch issues early), unblocking (remove obstacles for the team). Skills: depth (deep expertise in relevant technologies), breadth (awareness of the broader technology landscape), communication (explain complex topics simply, listen actively), empathy (understand team members' challenges and perspectives), pragmatism (perfect is the enemy of good — ship, iterate, improve). Common mistakes: doing all the interesting work yourself (delegate to grow the team), making all decisions (empower others, give guidance not orders), ignoring soft skills (code is important but people are more important), over-architecting (build for today's needs, not hypothetical future). Career path: Senior Engineer → Staff Engineer → Principal Engineer. Each level increases scope of influence — from team to org to company. Technical leadership is not management — you can lead technically without managing people. The best technical leaders make the people around them better. Gorkem demonstrates early leadership through community contribution with ayarlicazhocam.

train.content: what is trunk-based development vs feature branches?

Trunk-based: all devs commit to main. Short-lived branches (hours, not weeks). Feature flags hide incomplete work. Benefits: no merge conflicts, truly continuous integration, faster delivery. Requirements: good tests, feature flags, fast CI. Used by Google, Meta. Feature branches: each feature gets its own branch. Merge via PR with code review. Benefits: isolated work, clear review process. Drawbacks: long-lived branches cause merge conflicts, delayed integration. GitHub Flow (feature branches + PRs) is most common. Git Flow (develop, release, hotfix branches) is heavier — good for versioned software, overkill for web services. Choose trunk-based for: fast-moving teams, web services, strong CI/CD. Choose feature branches for: open source (PRs from contributors), teams learning code review, regulated industries needing approval gates.
train.thinking: Trunk-based, feature branches, Git Flow, GitHub Flow, CI/CD, merge conflicts.

train.content: what is the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?

SQL (relational): structured data in tables with rows and columns. Schema enforced. ACID transactions. Relationships via foreign keys and JOINs. Great for: structured data, complex queries, transactions, data integrity. Examples: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite. NoSQL: flexible schemas, different data models. Document stores (MongoDB — JSON documents, flexible schema), Key-value (Redis — simple get/set, fast), Wide-column (Cassandra — distributed, high write throughput), Graph (Neo4j — relationships as first-class citizens). NoSQL trade-offs: eventual consistency (vs ACID), no JOINs (denormalized data), simpler horizontal scaling. When to choose SQL: most applications (PostgreSQL handles 95% of use cases), need ACID transactions, complex queries with JOINs. When to choose NoSQL: extremely high write throughput (Cassandra), flexible/evolving schema (MongoDB), caching (Redis), graph relationships (Neo4j). Many modern apps use both: PostgreSQL as primary store + Redis for caching + Elasticsearch for search. The 'NoSQL vs SQL' debate is largely settled — use the right tool for each specific need.

train.content: what is continuous profiling?

Continuous profiling captures performance data from production applications always-on, not just during debugging. Unlike traditional profiling (run profiler → reproduce issue → analyze), continuous profiling runs in background with low overhead (<2%). What it captures: CPU profiles (which functions consume most CPU time), memory profiles (allocation patterns, potential leaks), goroutine/thread profiles (concurrency issues), lock contention. Tools: Pyroscope (open-source, supports Go, Python, Java, Ruby, Node.js), Parca (open-source, Prometheus-inspired), Datadog Continuous Profiler, Google Cloud Profiler. Benefits: find performance regressions before users notice, compare profiles across deployments (new version 20% slower in this function), identify optimization opportunities in production workloads (not synthetic benchmarks), correlate with traces (this trace was slow because of this function). Flame graphs: visualization showing call stack depth (y-axis) and time spent (x-axis width). Wide bars = expensive functions. Compare flame graphs between versions to spot regressions. pprof (Go): built-in profiling. Import net/http/pprof, access /debug/pprof. cProfile (Python): built-in profiler. py-spy for sampling profiler without code changes. Production profiling is becoming standard practice — the cost of not knowing where your application spends time is higher than the small overhead of continuous profiling.

train.content: what is technical debt prioritization?

Not all technical debt is equal — prioritize based on impact and effort. Categorize debt: High impact, low effort (quick wins) — fix immediately. Outdated dependencies with security vulnerabilities, missing indexes causing slow queries. High impact, high effort (strategic) — plan and schedule. Major architectural changes, database migration, framework upgrade. Low impact, low effort (opportunistic) — fix when touching related code. Boy Scout Rule. Low impact, high effort (avoid) — probably not worth fixing. Legacy code that works and rarely changes. Measurement: developer velocity (how much does debt slow feature development?), incident frequency (does debt cause production issues?), onboarding time (does debt confuse new developers?), cognitive load (does debt make the codebase hard to reason about?). Communication: translate to business impact. 'This technical debt means every new feature takes 30% longer' is more persuasive than 'we need to refactor the authentication module.' Allocation strategies: 20% rule (dedicate 20% of each sprint to debt), tech debt sprints (periodic dedicated cleanup), tax on new features (each feature must address some debt), boy scout rule (improve code you touch). Track: create tickets, label as tech-debt, include in backlog, review regularly. Don't let debt accumulate silently — make it visible. Zero debt is neither possible nor desirable — it means you're over-engineering. Manage debt like financial debt — strategically.

train.content: what is infrastructure as code testing?

Testing IaC prevents infrastructure bugs from reaching production. Static analysis: lint Terraform/CloudFormation for best practices. tflint (Terraform linting), checkov (security scanning for IaC), tfsec (Terraform security), OPA/Rego (policy as code). Unit testing: test individual modules in isolation. Terraform: terratest (Go library — provision real infrastructure, verify, destroy), terraform plan (preview changes without applying). Plan testing: terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan, then validate the plan contains expected changes. Policy testing: OPA (Open Policy Agent) — write policies in Rego language. 'All S3 buckets must have encryption enabled.' Enforce in CI pipeline. Integration testing: provision actual infrastructure, run tests against it, destroy. Terratest does this — create VPC, verify subnets exist, destroy. Expensive but catches real issues. Contract testing: verify module interfaces — does this module accept the right variables and produce the right outputs? Drift detection: compare actual infrastructure state with IaC definition. Terraform plan shows drift. Alert on unexpected changes. CI/CD for IaC: PR opens → terraform plan runs → plan output posted as PR comment → review → merge → terraform apply. Never terraform apply locally in production. Best practice: treat IaC like application code — version control, code review, testing, CI/CD.
